title: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar and the Mahad Satyagraha: Civic Equality and the Right to Water — 1927
summary: On March 20, 1927, Dr. B. R. Ambedkar led thousands to the Chawdar tank in Mahad, asserting that access to common public water is an inalienable fundamental human right.
keywords: Historical Dialogue 145: லிங்கனும் சிறுவனும்: “லிங்கனுக்கு வாழ்த்து!” — “உனக்கும் வாழ்த்து!”
full_text:
On March 20, 1927, the small town of Mahad in Maharashtra became the cradle of modern India's civil rights movement.

At the center of the town lay the Chawdar Tank. Under prevailing caste customs, stray cattle, birds, and animals were permitted free access to its waters, yet human beings belonging to the Depressed Classes were strictly forbidden from touching or drawing water from it. Though the Bombay Legislative Council had passed a resolution declaring public water bodies open to all, local orthodoxy refused to implement the law.

On that morning, Dr. B. R. Ambedkar led thousands of peaceful delegates through the streets of Mahad. Reaching the banks of the Chawdar Tank, Ambedkar walked down the stone steps, cupped the clear water in his bare hands, and drank. Thousands followed his lead, asserting their civic dignity.

Addressing the assembly, Ambedkar crystallized the historic meaning of their act:
"We have not assembled at the Chawdar Tank merely to quench our physical thirst. We do not imagine that drinking this water will grant us immortality. We are here to establish our fundamental human right! We are here to declare to the world that we, too, are human beings endowed with the same dignity and rights as all others. Self-respect is the vital essence of life; without it, man is nothing!"

The Mahad Satyagraha transformed the struggle of marginalized communities from an appeal for charity into an unyielding assertion of constitutional human rights.

moral: Access to common natural resources and equal human dignity are inalienable rights that no orthodoxy can legitimately deny.
